claim: Sepsis is described as a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infections.
source: Sepsis is described as a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infections (Singer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singer et al., 2016

claim: Inflammation-driven metabolic reprogramming and its consequences in the immune compartment have been investigated extensively.
source: Inflammation-driven metabolic reprogramming and its consequences in the immune compartment have been investigated extensively (Hu et al., 2022; Arner and Rathmell, 2023; Mohammadnezhad et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2022; Arner and Rathmell, 2023; Mohammadnezhad et al., 2022

claim: The liver is a target for profound transcriptional and metabolic remodeling in response to polymicrobial sepsis.
source: We have previously shown the liver is a target for profound transcriptional and metabolic remodeling in response to polymicrobial sepsis.
evidence: Supported by authors' previous work referenced in the text

claim: Sepsis induces an alteration in mitochondrial function, TCA cycle remodeling, and hepatic lipid accumulation.
source: Specifically, we observe an alteration in mitochondrial function, TCA cycle remodeling, and hepatic lipid accumulation following sepsis (Mainali et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mainali et al., 2021

claim: Hepatic metabolic dysregulation contributes to altered systemic metabolism during sepsis.
source: Additionally, we have extended these findings to show that hepatic metabolic dysregulation contributes to altered systemic metabolism during sepsis (Oh et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oh et al., 2022

claim: Hepatic steatosis is induced during sepsis and is an independent predictor of 30 day mortality.
source: Our previous work is consistent with human studies indicating hepatic steatosis is induced during sepsis and an independent predictor of 30 day mortality (Hou et al., 2021; Koskinas et al., 2008; Guirgis et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hou et al., 2021; Koskinas et al., 2008; Guirgis et al., 2021

claim: Inhibition of PPARα within hepatocytes exacerbates sepsis-induced pathology.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of the master lipid sensor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) within hepatocytes exacerbates sepsis-induced pathology (Paumelle et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paumelle et al., 2019

claim: Itaconate is produced by the decarboxylation of cis-aconitate via aconitase decarboxylase 1 (Acod1).
source: Itaconate is one such metabolite produced by the decarboxylation of cis-aconitate via aconitase decarboxylase 1 (Acod1), also known as immuno-responsive gene 1 (Irg1) (Bentley and Thiessen, 1957; Bonnarme et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bentley and Thiessen, 1957; Bonnarme et al., 1995

claim: Itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via the induction of Nrf214 and ATF3.
source: Numerous studies have shown itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via multiple mechanisms including the induction of Nrf214 and ATF3 (Bambouskova et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bambouskova et al., 2018

claim: Itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH).
source: Numerous studies have shown itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via multiple mechanisms including the induction of Nrf214 and ATF3 (Bambouskova et al., 2018), as well as inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) (Lampropoulou et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lampropoulou et al., 2016

claim: Itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via inhibition of NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Numerous studies have shown itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via multiple mechanisms including the induction of Nrf214 and ATF3 (Bambouskova et al., 2018), as well as inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) (Lampropoulou et al., 2016), NLRP3 inflammasome (Hooftman et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hooftman et al., 2020

claim: Itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via inhibition of glycolysis.
source: Numerous studies have shown itaconate exerts anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative effects via multiple mechanisms including the induction of Nrf214 and ATF3 (Bambouskova et al., 2018), as well as inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) (Lampropoulou et al., 2016), NLRP3 inflammasome (Hooftman et al., 2020), glycolysis (Peace and O'Neill, 2022; Liao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peace and O'Neill, 2022; Liao et al., 2019

claim: The therapeutic potential of itaconate derivatives has shown promise in a variety of pre-clinical models of inflammatory diseases.
source: Additionally, the therapeutic potential of itaconate derivatives has shown promise in a variety of pre-clinical models of inflammatory diseases (Peace and O'Neill, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peace and O'Neill, 2022

claim: Sepsis elicits significant accumulation of itaconate within hepatocytes.
source: We have previously demonstrated sepsis elicits significant accumulation of itaconate within hepatocytes (Mainali et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mainali et al., 2021

claim: Sepsis induces hepatic lipid accumulation in WT mice as shown by increased oil red O staining.
source: Consistent with our previous reports (Mainali et al., 2021), we find sepsis-induced hepatic lipid accumulation as shown by increased oil red O staining and quantification in WT mice (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a-b and citation to previous work

claim: Septic Acod1 KO mice exhibited enhanced lipid droplet accumulation compared to WT littermates.
source: Remarkably, septic Acod1 KO mice exhibited enhanced lipid droplet accumulation and significantly higher triglyceride levels compared to WT littermates (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a-b

claim: Septic Acod1 KO mice exhibited significantly higher triglyceride levels compared to WT littermates.
source: Remarkably, septic Acod1 KO mice exhibited enhanced lipid droplet accumulation and significantly higher triglyceride levels compared to WT littermates (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a-b

claim: Female Acod1 KO mice injected with endotoxin exhibited a higher degree of lipid droplet accumulation compared to endotoxin-treated WT littermates.
source: Parallel to male mice, female Acod1 KO mice injected with endotoxin exhibited a higher degree of lipid droplet accumulation compared to endotoxin-treated WT littermates as demonstrated by enhanced BODIY staining in liver sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Primary hepatocytes pretreated with 4-OI demonstrate lower oleate-induced lipid droplet formation.
source: Utilizing the cell-permeable itaconate derivative, 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI), we find that both primary hepatocytes and AML12 cells pretreated with 4-OI (250 μM) demonstrate lower oleate-induced lipid droplet formation (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c

claim: AML12 cells pretreated with 4-OI demonstrate lower oleate-induced lipid droplet formation.
source: Utilizing the cell-permeable itaconate derivative, 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI), we find that both primary hepatocytes and AML12 cells pretreated with 4-OI (250 μM) demonstrate lower oleate-induced lipid droplet formation (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c

claim: Itaconate acts as an anti-steatotic metabolite within the liver both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate itaconate acts as an anti-steatotic metabolite within the liver both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: 4-OI treatment results in enhanced expression of proteins involved with oxidative phosphorylation such as COX7A2L, ATPAF1, and NDUFAB1.
source: Notably, we find enhanced expression of proteins involved with oxidative phosphorylation such as COX7A2L, ATPAF1, NDUFAB1, as well as the fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes ACSL3-5, CPT1a, CPT2, and ACAA2 following 4-OI stimulation (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 2b

claim: 4-OI treatment results in enhanced expression of fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes ACSL3-5, CPT1a, CPT2, and ACAA2.
source: Notably, we find enhanced expression of proteins involved with oxidative phosphorylation such as COX7A2L, ATPAF1, NDUFAB1, as well as the fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes ACSL3-5, CPT1a, CPT2, and ACAA2 following 4-OI stimulation (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Enhanced expression of CPT1a, CPT2, and SLC25a20 were verified via western blot analysis following 4-OI stimulation.
source: Enhanced expression of CPT1a, CPT2, and SLC25a20 were verified in independent experiments via western blot analysis (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Loss of Acod1 significantly decreased the expression of CPT1a, CPT2, and SLC25a20 in endotoxin-treated mice.
source: Assessing the protein expression of these enzymes in endotoxin-treated WT and Acod1 KO mice revealed loss of Acod1 significantly decreased the expression of CPT1a, CPT2, and SLC25a20 (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Etomoxir treatment reverses the anti-steatotic effects of 4-OI resulting in lipid droplet formation similar to oleate-loaded control cells.
source: We find etomoxir treatment reverses the anti-steatotic effects of 4-OI resulting in lipid droplet formation similar to oleate-loaded control cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Upregulation of β-oxidation enzymes in response to itaconate affords its anti-steatotic effects.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrates upregulation of β-oxidation enzymes in response to itaconate, which affords, at least in part, its anti-steatotic effects.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing etomoxir reverses 4-OI effects

claim: 4-OI stimulation significantly extended the half-life of CPT1a protein.
source: CPT1a displayed a prolonged half-life of about 24 hr in vehicle-treated cells (Figure 3a). In contrast, stimulation with 4-OI significantly extended the half-life of CPT1a protein (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiment data shown in Figure 3a

claim: 4-OI stimulation drastically reduced levels of CPT1a polyubiquitination.
source: However, in the presence of MG132 we observe robust polyubiquitination of CPT1a in the vehicle-treated group (Figure 3b). In contrast, 4-OI stimulation drastically reduced levels of CPT1a polyubiquitination (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3b

claim: 4-OI interferes with CPT1a ubiquitination promoting its stabilization.
source: Taken together, our data indicate 4-OI interferes with CPT1a ubiquitination promoting its stabilization.
evidence: Inferred from ubiquitination and protein stability data

claim: Hepatic proteins are subject to itaconation.
source: In-gel fluorescence of both Raw Macrophages and AML12 cells treated with iTalk display a banding pattern compared to vehicle-treated cells (Figure 3c). Additionally, pre-treatment with the competitive inhibitor 4-OI blocks this banding pattern, indicating the specificity of the iTalk probe for itaconation (Figure 3c). These data indicate that hepatic proteins are indeed subject to itaconation.
evidence: Supported by iTalk labeling data shown in Figure 3c

claim: CPT1a was not identified as a hepatic itaconation substrate.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis and previous reports, we did not identify CPT1a as a hepatic itaconation substrate.
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry analysis of iTalk-labeled proteins

claim: Proteins involved in protein ubiquitination show enrichment in the itaconation group.
source: Additionally, we found proteins involved in protein ubiquitination to show enrichment in the itaconation group (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of iTalk-enriched proteins shown in Figure 3d

claim: Itaconation of ubiquitin ligases and proteasome components may confer the stabilizing effects of itaconate on CPT1a.
source: We hypothesize itaconation of ubiquitin ligases and proteasome components may confer the stabilizing effects of itaconate on CPT1a.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on iTalk proteomic data

claim: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) contributes to non-shivering thermogenesis through oxidation of fatty acids and activation of UCP1.
source: While white adipose tissues function to store excess energy in the form of triglycerides, brown adipose tissue (BAT) are metabolically active adipose depots which contribute to non-shivering thermogenesis (Kajimura et al., 2015). This is achieved, in part, through oxidation of fatty acids and activation of UCP1 (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kajimura et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2015

claim: A decrease in body temperature during sepsis is an independent predictor of mortality.
source: A decrease in body temperature during sepsis is an independent predictor of mortality (Rumbus et al., 2017; Fatteh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rumbus et al., 2017; Fatteh et al., 2021

claim: WT mice display a significant drop in body temperature in response to LPS treatment, peaking at 12 hr and returning to near baseline by 24 hr.
source: WT display a significant drop in body temperature in response to LPS treatment, peaking at 12 hr and returning to near baseline by 24 hr (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by body temperature measurements shown in Figure 4a

claim: Acod1 KO mice have a significantly more dramatic drop in body temperature following LPS treatment compared to WT littermates.
source: We find Acod1 KO mice have a significantly more dramatic drop in body temperature following LPS treatment compared to their WT littermates (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by body temperature measurements shown in Figure 4a

claim: Acod1 deficient mice show impairment in UCP1 gene and protein levels following endotoxin treatment.
source: We find impairment in UCP1 gene and protein levels in Acod1 deficient mice following endotoxin treatment, independent of PGC1α expression (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 4b-d

claim: The BAT of endotoxin-challenged Acod1 KO mice was larger in weight compared to LPS-injected WT septic mice.
source: Furthermore, the BAT of endotoxin-challenged Acod1 KO mice was larger in weight compared to LPS-injected WT septic mice (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by BAT weight measurements shown in Figure 4e

claim: There is an impairment in UCP1-driven thermogenesis in the BAT of Acod1-deficient mice following an inflammatory challenge.
source: In summary, these data indicate an impairment in UCP1-driven thermogenesis in the BAT of Acod1-deficient mice following an inflammatory challenge.
evidence: Inferred from body temperature and UCP1 expression data

claim: Impaired BAT fatty acid oxidation may be mediated by the larger BAT depot in inflamed Acod1 KO mice.
source: Furthermore, our data indicate this could be mediated by impaired BAT fatty acid oxidation, as evidenced by the larger BAT depot in inflamed Acod1 KO mice.
evidence: Speculative inference based on BAT weight data

claim: A global shift in systemic fuel preference from glucose to fatty acid oxidation occurs in response to CLP-induced sepsis.
source: We have previously reported a global shift in systemic fuel preference from glucose to fatty acid oxidation in response to CLP-induced sepsis (Oh et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oh et al., 2022

claim: Acod1 KO mice favor glucose oxidation over fatty acids under baseline conditions.
source: However, it is known that Acod1 KO mice favor glucose oxidation over fatty acids under baseline conditions (Frieler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frieler et al., 2022

claim: WT septic mice demonstrated a shift in fuel preference indicated by a decrease in RER from about 1 to 0.7.
source: Consistent with our previous study (Oh et al., 2022), WT septic mice demonstrated a shift in fuel preference indicated by a decrease in RER from about 1–0.7 (Figure 5e–h), signifying a higher reliance on fatty acid oxidation over glucose utilization.
evidence: Supported by RER measurements shown in Figure 5e-h and citation to Oh et al., 2022

claim: Acod1 KO mice had a decrease in RER following LPS treatment, but not to the same extent as WT counterparts.
source: Interestingly, we found Acod1 KO mice had a decrease in RER following LPS treatment, however, not to the same extent as their WT-type counterparts (Figure 5g, h), indicating itaconate deficiency leads to a subtle defect of systemic fat utilization.
evidence: Supported by RER measurements shown in Figure 5g-h

claim: Itaconate deficiency leads to a subtle defect of systemic fat utilization.
source: Interestingly, we found Acod1 KO mice had a decrease in RER following LPS treatment, however, not to the same extent as their WT-type counterparts (Figure 5g, h), indicating itaconate deficiency leads to a subtle defect of systemic fat utilization.
evidence: Inferred from RER data showing less dramatic shift in Acod1 KO mice

claim: Itaconate is a central modulator of lipid metabolism during the course of overt inflammation.
source: Our studies identify itaconate as a central modulator of lipid metabolism during the course of overt inflammation.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented

claim: Itaconate may enhance lipid clearing in the liver through the stabilization of mitochondrial fatty acid uptake enzyme CPT1a.
source: Specifically, we show itaconate may enhance lipid clearing in the liver through the stabilization of mitochondrial fatty acid uptake enzyme CPT1a.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on CPT1a stabilization and ubiquitination data

claim: Itaconate has been shown to play a role in regulating the β-oxidation of fatty acids to fuel OXPHOS in hepatocytes from mouse models of NAFLD.
source: Previously, it has been reported that itaconate plays a role in regulating the β-oxidation of fatty acids to fuel OXPHOS. This has been observed in various cell types, including hepatocytes from mouse models of NAFDL
evidence: Supported by reference to previous literature

claim: Itaconate has been shown to play a role in regulating the β-oxidation of fatty acids to fuel OXPHOS in tissue-resident macrophages in peritoneal tumors.
source: This has been observed in various cell types, including hepatocytes from mouse models of NAFDL, tissue-resident macrophages in peritoneal tumors (Weiss et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2018

claim: Itaconate has been shown to play a role in regulating the β-oxidation of fatty acids to fuel OXPHOS in macrophages from zebrafish.
source: This has been observed in various cell types, including hepatocytes from mouse models of NAFDL, tissue-resident macrophages in peritoneal tumors (Weiss et al., 2018), macrophages from zebrafish (Hall et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hall et al., 2013

claim: Itaconate has been shown to play a role in regulating the β-oxidation of fatty acids to fuel OXPHOS in T cell subsets Th17- and Treg- polarizing T cells.
source: This has been observed in various cell types, including hepatocytes from mouse models of NAFDL, tissue-resident macrophages in peritoneal tumors (Weiss et al., 2018), macrophages from zebrafish (Hall et al., 2013) as well as T cell subsets Th17- and Treg- polarizing T cells (Aso et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aso et al., 2023

claim: Itaconyl-CoA can cause inactivation of vitamin B12.
source: We hypothesize this is due to the inactivation of vitamin B12 by itaconyl-CoA, resulting from itaconate activation (Cordes and Metallo, 2021; Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cordes and Metallo, 2021; Shen et al., 2017

claim: Deficiency in B12 has been found to induce cholesterol biosynthesis by limiting SAM and modulating the methylation of SREBF1 and LDLR genes.
source: Interestingly deficiency in B12 has been found to induce cholesterol biosynthesis by limiting SAM and modulating the methylation of SREBF1 and LDLR genes (Adaikalakoteswari et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adaikalakoteswari et al., 2015

claim: Alteration in intracellular SAM abundance and reduction in SAM/SAH ratio by itaconate was found to influence TH17/Treg cell differentiation as a result of tri-methylation of histone H3 protein-induced epigenetic reprogramming.
source: Additionally, alteration in intracellular SAM abundance and reduction in SAM/SAH ratio by itaconate was found to influence TH17 /Treg cell differentiation as a result of tri-methylation of histone H3 protein-induced epigenetic reprogramming (Aso et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aso et al., 2023

claim: Endotoxin induces the expression of Acod1 in brown adipose tissue (BAT).
source: Furthermore, they demonstrated endotoxin induces the expression of Acod1 in brown adipose tissue (BAT).
evidence: Supported by reference to Frieler et al. study

claim: Exogenous 4-OI administration improved body temperature and clinical scores in septic mice.
source: A previous study demonstrated improved body temperature and clinical scores in septic mice upon exogenous 4-OI administration (Mills et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mills et al., 2018

claim: BAT utilizes hepatic-derived acylcarnitines released in response to cold stress.
source: Research has demonstrated that inter-organ crosstalk between BAT and the liver is essential to elicit non-shivering thermogenesis. Specifically, BAT utilizes hepatic-derived acylcarnitines released in response to cold stress (Simcox et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Simcox et al., 2017

claim: There is a reliance on hepatic CPT1 function to mediate cold stress-induced acylcarnitine secretion.
source: Intriguingly, these studies demonstrated a reliance on hepatic CPT1 function to mediate cold stress-induced acylcarnitine secretion (Simcox et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simcox et al., 2017

claim: The onset of hypothermia in sepsis is considered a predictor of mortality in murine models.
source: This is important, as clinically and in murine models of sepsis, the onset of hypothermia is observed and considered a predictor of mortality (Lewis et al., 2016; Kushimoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2016; Kushimoto et al., 2013

claim: Itaconate upregulates NRF2 due to the alkylation of cysteine residues of KEAP1.
source: The first is the classical upregulation of NRF2 due to the alkylation of cysteine residues of KEAP123, which functions as an adaptor of the Cul3-based ubiquitin E3 ligase complex. This covalent modification promotes the dissociation of KEAP1 from CUL3 to inhibit the conjugation of ubiquitin onto the N-terminal domain of NRF2 (Mills et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2018; Canning et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mills et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2018; Canning et al., 2015

claim: 4-OI negatively regulates osteoclastogenesis and inflammatory response by suppressing E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase HRD1 to activate Nrf2 signaling.
source: Additionally, 4-OI has been shown to negatively regulate osteoclastogenesis and inflammatory response by suppressing E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase HRD1 to activate Nrf2 signaling (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2019

claim: Itaconate interacts with multiple components involved in proteasomal turnover of proteins.
source: Our data extends these findings and indicates an interaction between itaconate and multiple components involved in proteasomal turnover of proteins.
evidence: Based on iTalk proteomic analysis showing enrichment of ubiquitination pathway proteins

claim: Interventions aimed at regulating the Acod1/itaconate axis may hold potential therapeutic advantages in regulating dyslipidemia at both the local and systemic levels observed during sepsis.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that interventions aimed at regulating the Acod1/itaconate axis may hold potential therapeutic advantages in regulating dyslipidemia at both the local and systemic levels observed during sepsis.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on all experimental findings

claim: Itaconate has the ability to modulate lipid metabolism.
source: Given itaconate accumulates within hepatocytes during sepsis and previous reports demonstrating the ability of itaconate to modulate lipid metabolism (Frieler et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020; Hall et al., 2013; Chu et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Frieler et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020; Hall et al., 2013; Chu et al., 2022

claim: Acod1 is also known as immuno-responsive gene 1 (Irg1).
source: Itaconate is one such metabolite produced by the decarboxylation of cis-aconitate via aconitase decarboxylase 1 (Acod1), also known as immuno-responsive gene 1 (Irg1) (Bentley and Thiessen, 1957; Bonnarme et al., 1995).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citations

claim: One primary metabolic manifestation of inflammation is the diversion of cis-aconitate within the TCA cycle to synthesize the immunometabolite itaconate.
source: One primary metabolic manifestation of inflammation is the diversion of cis-aconitate within the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle to synthesize the immunometabolite itaconate.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about inflammation-induced metabolic changes

claim: Itaconate is well established to possess immunomodulatory and metabolic effects within myeloid cells and lymphocytes.
source: Itaconate is well established to possess immunomodulatory and metabolic effects within myeloid cells and lymphocytes
evidence: Established scientific knowledge based on previous literature

claim: The effects of itaconate in other organ systems during sepsis remain less clear.
source: however, its effects in other organ systems during sepsis remain less clear.
evidence: Statement about gap in current knowledge

claim: Acod1 KO mice develop a heightened level of hepatic steatosis when induced with polymicrobial sepsis.
source: We find itaconate aids in lipid metabolism during sepsis. Specifically, Acod1 KO mice develop a heightened level of hepatic steatosis when induced with polymicrobial sepsis.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from Figure 1

claim: Proteomics analysis reveals enhanced expression of enzymes involved in fatty acid oxidation following 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI) treatment in vitro.
source: Proteomics analysis reveals enhanced expression of enzymes involved in fatty acid oxidation in following 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI) treatment in vitro.
evidence: Summary of proteomic findings from Figure 2

claim: Itaconate stabilizes the expression of the mitochondrial fatty acid uptake enzyme CPT1a, mediated by its hypoubiquitination.
source: Downstream analysis reveals itaconate stabilizes the expression of the mitochondrial fatty acid uptake enzyme CPT1a, mediated by its hypoubiquitination.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 3 on CPT1a stability and ubiquitination

claim: Chemoproteomic analysis revealed itaconate interacts with proteins involved in protein ubiquitination as a potential mechanism underlying its stabilizing effect on CPT1a.
source: Chemoproteomic analysis revealed itaconate interacts with proteins involved in protein ubiquitination as a potential mechanism underlying its stabilizing effect on CPT1a.
evidence: Summary of iTalk proteomic findings from Figure 3d

claim: Itaconate deficiency triggers a hypothermic response following endotoxin stimulation, potentially mediated by brown adipose tissue (BAT) dysfunction.
source: From a systemic perspective, we find itaconate deficiency triggers a hypothermic response following endotoxin stimulation, potentially mediated by brown adipose tissue (BAT) dysfunction.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 4 with speculative mechanism

claim: Acod1 KO mice rely more heavily on carbohydrates versus fatty acid sources for systemic fuel utilization in response to endotoxin treatment.
source: Finally, by use of metabolic cage studies, we demonstrate Acod1 KO mice rely more heavily on carbohydrates versus fatty acid sources for systemic fuel utilization in response to endotoxin treatment.
evidence: Summary of metabolic cage findings from Figure 5

claim: Itaconate has a novel metabolic role in modulating fatty acid oxidation during polymicrobial sepsis.
source: Our data reveal a novel metabolic role of itaconate in modulating fatty acid oxidation during polymicrobial sepsis.
evidence: Overall conclusion based on all experimental data

claim: CPT1a was shown to interact with itaconate via the biorthogonal probe iTalk in macrophages.
source: This is based on previous reports in macrophages in which CPT1a was shown to interact with itaconate via the biorthogonal probe iTalk (Qin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qin et al., 2020

claim: Itaconate deficiency may hinder hepatic acylcarnitine production due to impairment in CPT1a expression.
source: These findings in conjunction with previous literature may provide a potential physiological mechanism by which itaconate deficiency hinders hepatic acylcarnitine production due to impairment in CPT1a expression.
evidence: Speculative mechanism inferred from experimental data and literature

claim: Endogenous itaconate has a protective role in regulating adipocyte metabolism through altering glucose homeostasis, lipolysis, and adipogenesis during HFD-induced obesity.
source: Frieler et al. recently uncovered a protective role of endogenous itaconate in regulating adipocyte metabolism through altering glucose homeostasis, lipolysis, and adipogenesis during HFD-induced obesity (Frieler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frieler et al., 2022
